scams.description: Every restaurant on Mont-Saint-Michel is described as a tourist trap with shockingly bad service, mediocre food, and excessive prices. With no repeat customers, restaurants have zero incentive to provide quality. Visitors report paying 4.50 euros for a 500ml water bottle, 9.80 euros for a small beer, 7 euros per glass of wine, and 3.50 euros for low-quality crepes.
scams.avoidance: Pack your own food and water before arriving. Eat breakfast before visiting and dinner after leaving. Coffee or aperitifs are acceptable for the experience, but avoid full meals. Visit the fishing port of Cancale nearby for excellent seafood at fair prices.
scams.location: Grande Rue restaurants, all restaurants on Mont-Saint-Michel island

scams.name: Overpriced Parking Lot
scams.description: The official parking lot charges inflated prices with poor signage about costs before entry. Visitors report paying 14-25 euros for parking, with one person charged 17 euros for just 30 minutes and another 9.80 euros for less than 2 hours in an empty car park. The pricing feels exploitative given there is no alternative and visitors have no choice once they've driven there.
scams.avoidance: Check current parking rates online before visiting. Budget 15-20 euros for parking in your trip costs. Consider taking public transport or organized tours instead. Arrive early or late to minimize parking time.
scams.location: Official Mont-Saint-Michel parking area, P1 main parking lot

scams.name: Unlicensed Bay Crossing Danger
scams.description: The bay around Mont-Saint-Michel contains deadly quicksand pockets and experiences extreme tides that rise at speeds up to 6 km/hour - faster than a person can run. Tourists attempting to cross the bay without certified guides have died or required helicopter rescue after becoming trapped in quicksand as tides rushed in. In 2019 alone, multiple rescues were needed including one helicopter extraction.
scams.avoidance: NEVER enter the bay without a certified guide from the Prefecture de la Manche. Book official bay crossing tours through the tourism office. Check tide schedules before visiting. There are only 67 officially authorized guides - verify credentials.
scams.location: Mont-Saint-Michel Bay, tidal flats around the island, areas between parking and island

scams.name: Worthless Museum Trap
scams.description: Mont-Saint-Michel has several small private museums that charge 9 euros each or 18 euros for a package to visit multiple museums. Visitors describe them as dusty, dilapidated, with shabby exhibits in tiny rooms that are poorly presented. Three of the four museums have been called 'a disgrace' with dirt, mold on walls, and no real historical interest. They exist purely to extract money from tourists.
scams.avoidance: Skip all private museums on the island. The only worthwhile paid attraction is the Abbey itself (13 euros). Read reviews before paying any entrance fee. The free walking experience and architecture are the real attractions.
scams.location: Musee Historique, small museums on Grande Rue, museum complex on the island

scams.name: Candy Shop Overcharging
scams.description: Several candy and sweets shops on the main street employ deceptive pricing to overcharge tourists. Prices are listed at 8 euros per 100 grams (double the typical tourist area rate of 4 euros). Visitors report being ripped off for as much as 31 euros for a bag of sweets. Some shops use aggressive sales tactics, pressuring customers to pay after they've already filled a bag.
scams.avoidance: Ask for total price before filling any bag. Calculate the per-gram cost before selecting items. Don't feel obligated to buy if prices seem excessive. Buy sweets in mainland towns instead.
scams.location: Candy shops on Grande Rue, sweet shops along main street

scams.name: Crowded Street Theft
scams.description: Mont-Saint-Michel's single narrow street becomes extremely congested, especially from 10:30am to 5pm in peak season. The crushing crowds create ideal conditions for pickpockets who exploit tourists distracted by sights and jostled by crowds. Items left unattended - including wheelchairs, strollers, and bags at the abbey entrance where they must be left - can easily be stolen.
scams.avoidance: Visit early morning (before 10am) or evening (after 5pm) to avoid worst crowds. Wear crossbody bags in front of your body. Keep valuables in front pockets or money belt. Never leave bags unattended even briefly.
scams.location: Grande Rue (main street), narrow passages, Abbey entrance area, shuttle bus queues

scams.name: Parking Lot Vehicle Break-In
scams.description: Thieves target vehicles in the Mont-Saint-Michel parking lot, particularly rental cars identifiable by stickers or foreign plates. They watch tourists rearrange luggage in the lot (revealing valuables), then break into cars while owners spend hours visiting the island. This is part of a wider pattern of tourist parking lot thefts across Normandy.
scams.avoidance: Move valuables to trunk BEFORE arriving at the parking lot. Never rearrange luggage visibly in the lot. Remove rental company stickers from your vehicle. Park in high-traffic areas near the entrance.
scams.location: Mont-Saint-Michel parking lot, remote sections of parking area

scams.name: Hotel Overbooking Scam
scams.description: Hotels on Mont-Saint-Michel (mostly owned by one family/company with monopoly pricing power) have been reported to overbook rooms and then relocate guests to inferior mainland hotels at the last minute. Visitors receive emails about 'overbooking' and forced relocation to distant hotels at the same premium price, suspecting they were bumped for higher-paying tour groups.
scams.avoidance: Book well in advance and get written confirmation. Consider staying in mainland hotels intentionally - they offer better value. Book directly with hotels rather than through aggregators. Have backup accommodation options researched.
scams.location: Hotels on Mont-Saint-Michel island, L'Auberge Saint Pierre, Poulard Group hotels

scams.name: Tide Timing Trap
scams.description: Tourists often plan visits around seeing spectacular high tides but don't understand tide mechanics. High tides reaching 14 meters can occur, but they don't happen every day. Conversely, those who don't check tide schedules may be caught off-guard by rapidly rising water on the causeway or bay areas. The incoming tide can isolate visitors or trap them against walls.
scams.avoidance: Check tide schedules online before visiting (available on tourism website). Understand that exceptional tides only occur a few times yearly. Time your visit for 2 hours before high tide for best experience. Never walk the bay without awareness of tide timing.
scams.location: Causeway to Mont-Saint-Michel, bay surrounding the island, lower ramparts

scams.name: Tram Pickpocketing
scams.description: Montpellier's tram system is a prime hunting ground for organized pickpocket teams. Thieves work in groups during busy periods, especially during boarding and exiting when passengers are distracted and pressed together. One person creates a distraction or blocks movement while accomplices slip hands into bags and pockets. The crime happens in seconds, with perpetrators exiting at the next stop before victims realize anything is missing.
scams.avoidance: Wear bags zipped and close to your body in front. Keep hands on your belongings during boarding and exiting. Avoid placing phones or wallets in back pockets. Stay alert at busy stops like Comedie and Gare Saint-Roch.
scams.location: Tram Line 1 & 2, Gare Saint-Roch tram stop, Comedie tram stop, Place de l'Europe tram stop

scams.name: Place de la Comedie Pickpocketing
scams.description: Place de la Comedie, Montpellier's grand central square, attracts tourists and thieves alike. Pickpockets blend into the crowds around the iconic Three Graces fountain, targeting distracted visitors taking photos or sitting at outdoor cafes. Teams often work together - one distracts by asking for directions while another steals valuables. The open, busy nature of the square provides easy escape routes.
scams.avoidance: Keep bags on your lap or looped around chair legs at cafes. Be wary of anyone approaching with distractions. Don't leave phones or wallets on cafe tables. Stay alert while taking photos.
scams.location: Place de la Comedie, Three Graces Fountain area, Opera Comedie entrance area, cafe terraces

scams.name: Gare Saint-Roch Train Station Theft
scams.description: Montpellier's main train station is a hotspot for opportunistic theft targeting travelers burdened with luggage. Thieves observe arriving tourists who appear lost or confused, then strike when victims are distracted checking schedules, buying tickets, or managing bags. The area between the station and nearby tram stops is particularly risky. At night, the station vicinity has a rougher reputation.
scams.avoidance: Keep luggage close and in sight at all times. Don't appear lost - research your route before arriving. Use secure luggage with locks. Avoid lingering in the station area at night.
scams.location: Montpellier Saint-Roch train station, station entrance hall, platforms, tram stop outside station

scams.name: TGV Train Luggage Theft
scams.description: Thieves board TGV trains during brief station stops, posing as passengers. They position themselves with views of the luggage racks and wait for any distraction. Working in teams, one person engages the victim in conversation while the other grabs luggage from the rack and exits just before the doors close. With up to 400 such incidents monthly on French trains, this is a well-organized crime.
scams.avoidance: Keep valuables and essentials in a small bag you keep with you. Use cable locks to secure luggage to racks. Sit where you can see your luggage. Stay alert during station stops.
scams.location: TGV trains to/from Montpellier, luggage racks on trains, during station stops

scams.name: Fake Petition / Deaf Charity Scam
scams.description: Scammers approach tourists with clipboards, often pretending to be deaf-mute and collecting signatures for a fake charity. The petition is typically written in English to target foreign visitors. While you're distracted reading or signing, accomplices pickpocket you. If you sign, they demand a donation and can become aggressive when refused. The petition itself is worthless and no charity ever receives any funds.
scams.avoidance: Firmly say 'Non merci' and keep walking without slowing down. Never sign anything on the street. Don't engage in conversation. Keep hands on your belongings when approached.
scams.location: Place de la Comedie, Esplanade de l'Europe, tourist attractions, near cafes and restaurants

scams.name: Gold Ring Scam
scams.description: A stranger bends down near you and picks up what appears to be a gold ring, asking if you dropped it. When you say no, they examine it and claim it's marked '18k gold' and must be valuable. They offer to sell it for a fraction of its supposed worth, or guilt you into giving them a 'finder's fee.' The ring is worthless brass, and while you're engaged, an accomplice may be pickpocketing you.
scams.avoidance: Simply say 'no' and walk away without engaging. Don't examine or touch the ring. Keep moving and maintain awareness of your surroundings. Be aware that accomplices may be nearby.
scams.location: Place de la Comedie, Esplanade Charles de Gaulle, pedestrian streets in the Ecusson, near tourist attractions

scams.name: Taxi Overcharging / Broken Meter Scam
scams.description: Some taxi drivers target tourists by claiming the meter is broken and quoting inflated flat rates, taking unnecessarily long routes, or failing to reset the meter to the base fare before starting. The airport to city center trip should cost approximately 35 euros during the day and 42 euros at night, but unsuspecting tourists may pay significantly more. Drivers may also refuse to provide receipts.
scams.avoidance: Know approximate fares before traveling (airport to center: ~35 euros day, ~42 euros night). Insist on using the meter and verify it starts at 2 euros. Track your route on Google Maps. Use official taxi stands or ride-hailing apps.
scams.location: Montpellier-Mediterranee Airport, Gare Saint-Roch train station, hotel pickups, tourist areas

scams.name: Restaurant Bill Padding
scams.description: Some restaurants in tourist areas inflate bills with hidden charges or serve items not ordered. Common tactics include automatically bringing expensive bottled water instead of offering free tap water, adding cover charges not mentioned on menus, or 'accidentally' adding extra items to the bill. Tourists who don't check bills carefully pay significantly more than they should.
scams.avoidance: Always request 'une carafe d'eau' for free tap water. Check menu prices before ordering. Review your bill carefully before paying. Know that service is included - tipping beyond rounding up is optional.
scams.location: Tourist restaurants near Place de la Comedie, Rue de l'Ancien Courrier, terrace restaurants in Ecusson

scams.name: Rental Car Break-In
scams.description: Southern France has high rates of car break-ins, and rental cars are prime targets. Thieves identify rentals by company stickers, foreign plates, or luggage visible inside. They stake out tourist sites, knowing how long visitors typically stay, then break windows to steal bags and valuables. Rest stops along the A9 motorway approaching Montpellier are particularly notorious.
scams.avoidance: Never leave any belongings visible in the car - even empty bags look promising. Store items in the trunk before arriving at destinations. Remove or cover rental company stickers if possible. Use attended underground parking.
scams.location: Tourist attraction parking areas, beach parking at Palavas and Carnon, rest stops on A9 motorway

scams.name: ATM Skimming
scams.description: Criminals install skimming devices on ATMs that capture your card data and PIN. These devices are designed to look like part of the machine and are difficult to detect. Tourist areas are targeted because they process many foreign cards and victims are less familiar with how local ATMs should look. Your card details are then used to create clones or make fraudulent purchases.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside bank branches during business hours. Wiggle the card slot and keypad before inserting your card. Cover the keypad with your hand when entering your PIN. Monitor your account for unauthorized transactions.
scams.location: ATMs in tourist areas, street-facing ATMs near Place de la Comedie, train station ATMs

scams.name: Beach Grab / Swim-and-Steal
scams.description: When tourists go swimming in the Mediterranean, thieves watch for unattended belongings on the beach. They quickly grab bags, wallets, phones, and cameras while the owner is distracted in the water. The thief disappears into the crowd before the victim returns to their towel.
scams.avoidance: Never leave belongings unattended when swimming. Use your bag as a pillow when sunbathing. Bring a waterproof pouch to carry valuables while swimming. Travel with a companion who can watch your items.
scams.location: Promenade des Anglais beach, Public beaches, Private beach clubs

scams.name: Taxi Meter Manipulation / Overcharging
scams.description: Nice taxi drivers have a notorious reputation for overcharging tourists. Drivers may claim the meter is broken, quote inflated flat rates, obscure the meter with their hand to manipulate the fare, or take long routes. They often refuse credit cards and don't provide legally required receipts. Official fixed rates: Airport to Nice city center is €32, to Cannes is €85, to Monaco is €95.
scams.avoidance: Know official fixed rates before traveling. Always confirm the price before boarding. Insist on using the meter. Use Uber instead for transparent pricing. Always request a receipt.
scams.location: Nice Airport, Train Station (Gare de Nice-Ville), Hotel pickups, Tourist areas

scams.name: Airport Tram Ticket Overcharge
scams.description: At Nice Airport, ticket machines only sell a special 'airport ticket' priced at €10 round trip. This is three times the actual cost of a regular tram ticket (€1.70). The machines are designed to extract maximum money from tourists who don't know about cheaper alternatives.
scams.avoidance: Walk to Grand Arenas stop (one stop from airport) for regular ticket machines. Purchase tickets on the Lignes d'Azur mobile app. Be aware that regular fare is only €1.70.
scams.location: Nice Côte d'Azur Airport, Airport tram terminals

scams.name: Gold Ring Scam
scams.description: A stranger bends down near you and picks up what appears to be a gold ring, then asks if you dropped it. When you say no, they claim it's marked '14k gold' and must be valuable. They offer to sell it for a fraction of its 'worth' or demand a finder's fee. The ring is worthless brass. While engaging you, an accomplice may pickpocket you.
scams.avoidance: Simply say 'no' and walk away. Don't engage in conversation. Keep hands on your belongings. Be aware of accomplices nearby.
scams.location: Promenade des Anglais, Old Town (Vieux Nice), Near tourist attractions

scams.name: Petition / Deaf Charity Scam
scams.description: A young person approaches asking 'Speak English?' and presents a clipboard with a petition for a deaf charity. They use sign language to appear hearing-impaired. While you're distracted reading or signing, accomplices pickpocket you. If you sign, they demand a donation and become aggressive if refused.
scams.avoidance: Firmly say 'no' and keep walking. Never sign anything on the street. Keep hands on your belongings when approached.
scams.location: Promenade des Anglais, Old Town, Tourist attractions, Train station

scams.name: Bird Droppings / Mustard Scam
scams.description: One person secretly sprays liquid resembling bird droppings or mustard on your clothing from behind. Moments later, a 'helpful' stranger points out the mess and offers wet wipes to help clean you. While you're distracted removing your jacket or bag, accomplices steal your wallet, phone, or jewelry.
scams.avoidance: If you notice a stain, clean it yourself later. Never accept help from strangers for cleaning. Keep moving and find a safe private space. Hold onto your belongings tightly.
scams.location: Busy streets, Near tourist attractions, Public squares

scams.name: Vol à la Portière (Car Door Grab)
scams.description: Thieves target tourists in rental cars, identifiable by rental stickers or foreign plates. At traffic lights or in parking areas, they forcibly open the car door and snatch valuables from the seat. The crime happens in seconds, and the thieves disappear before victims can react.
scams.avoidance: Always lock car doors immediately upon entering. Keep windows rolled up, especially at traffic lights. Never leave valuables visible on seats. Consider removing rental company stickers.
scams.location: Traffic lights, Car parks, Parking garages, Rental car return areas

scams.name: Rental Car Break-In
scams.description: Thieves stake out tourist sites, watching visitors park rental cars (easily identified by stickers and foreign plates). Knowing average visit times for each attraction, they break into cars and steal luggage, bags, and electronics while owners are sightseeing. France has one of the highest car break-in rates in Western Europe.
scams.avoidance: Never leave any belongings visible in the car - even empty bags. Store everything in the trunk before arriving at your destination. Remove all tourist evidence (maps, guidebooks). Use attended parking when available.
scams.location: Tourist attractions, Scenic viewpoints, Parking garages, Street parking

scams.name: Fake Police Scam
scams.description: Criminals pose as plainclothes police, quickly flashing fake badges. They demand to see your wallet for 'inspection' due to alleged counterfeit currency concerns. While examining your wallet, they steal cash. Sometimes a 'tourist' accomplice first asks you to break a large bill, then the fake officer arrives claiming street money exchange is illegal.
scams.avoidance: Real police never ask to see your wallet - only ID documents. Ask to see official ID clearly. Insist on going to nearest police station. Never hand over your wallet to anyone on the street. Call 17 if suspicious.
scams.location: Tourist areas, Metro stations, Near bars at night

scams.name: Restaurant Overcharging / Water Scam
scams.description: Tourist restaurants employ tactics to overcharge visitors. Waiters bring expensive bottled water instead of offering free tap water. Bills include items not ordered or charge premium prices shown only on the 'tourist menu.' Some waiters insist on automatic gratuity. Restaurants may refuse to let solo diners order less than a full multi-course meal.
scams.avoidance: Request 'une carafe d'eau' (tap water) - it's free by law. Ask for the French menu and compare prices. Check the bill carefully. Know that tipping is not obligatory in France.
scams.location: Tourist restaurant areas, Promenade des Anglais restaurants, Old Town restaurants

scams.name: Public Transport Ticket Fine Trap
scams.description: Tourists buy tickets on Nice buses and trams but don't realize they must also validate (stamp) the ticket in a machine on board. Inspectors issue on-the-spot fines of €40 or more to tourists who have purchased tickets but failed to validate them. Bus drivers don't warn passengers about validation requirements.
scams.avoidance: Always validate your ticket immediately upon boarding. Listen for the 'beep' confirming validation. Watch what local passengers do. If unsure, ask the driver or another passenger.
scams.location: Trams, Buses, Train stations

scams.name: Grand Arenas Tram Stop Pickpocket
scams.description: Knowing that tourists go to Grand Arenas to avoid overpriced airport tickets, pickpockets (often teenage girls) target tired, luggage-laden visitors at ticket machines. One person offers to 'help' with the confusing ticket machine while an accomplice steals from your bag or pockets.
scams.avoidance: Politely decline all offers of help. Keep bags in front of you and secured. Be aware of your surroundings. Have a travel companion watch your belongings.
scams.location: Grand Arenas tram stop near airport

scams.name: Rose / Flower Seller Scam
scams.description: Vendors approach couples at restaurants offering a 'free' rose. Once you accept or touch it, they aggressively demand 10-20 euros. They exploit social pressure, especially with couples where one partner may feel embarrassed to refuse. They become persistent and confrontational if payment is refused.
scams.avoidance: Firmly say 'no' before touching anything. Put hands in pockets or cross arms. Don't feel guilty - this is a known scam. Ask restaurant staff to intervene if aggressive.
scams.location: Restaurant terraces, Promenade des Anglais, Romantic spots, Outdoor cafes

scams.name: ATM Skimming
scams.description: Criminals attach hidden card readers (skimmers) and fake keypads to ATMs to capture card details and PINs. In some cases, a false slot insert causes the card to jam; when you leave to seek help, the scammer retrieves your card. Card data is then used for fraudulent transactions or clone cards.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours. Wiggle the card slot before inserting - skimmers are loosely attached. Cover keypad when entering PIN. If card gets stuck, do NOT leave - call bank immediately. Enable transaction alerts on your cards.
scams.location: Standalone ATMs, Tourist area ATMs, ATMs in dimly lit areas

scams.name: Luxury Watch Theft
scams.description: The French Riviera has seen a surge in thefts of luxury watches. Thieves on scooters target tourists wearing expensive timepieces, pulling up alongside and forcibly removing watches. Some operate on foot, approaching in crowded areas to snatch watches off wrists. The attacks can be quick and violent.
scams.avoidance: Leave expensive watches at home or in hotel safe. If wearing a luxury watch, keep it covered with sleeves. Don't flash expensive jewelry in public. Consider travel insurance covering valuable items.
scams.location: Promenade des Anglais, Luxury hotel areas, Nice city center

scams.name: Vacation Rental Scam
scams.description: Scammers create fake listings on Airbnb, VRBO, or independent sites advertising attractive properties at below-market rates. After victims pay via wire transfer or outside the platform, they arrive to find the property doesn't exist, is occupied, or belongs to someone else. Some use stolen photos from legitimate listings.
scams.avoidance: Book only through official platforms. Never pay outside the platform. Do reverse image searches on property photos. Read reviews carefully. Use credit card for payments (easier to dispute).
scams.location: Online (before arrival)

scams.name: The Gold Ring Trick
scams.description: You're strolling along the Seine near Pont des Arts when a woman ahead of you bends down and holds up a shiny gold ring. 'Excusez-moi, is this yours? I just found it — pure gold, look!' She presses the ring into your hand before you can respond, examines it theatrically, and declares it's too big for her. Then comes the pivot: a hard-luck story about her sick child, and wouldn't you know it, could you spare a few euros since you're so lucky to have found this valuable ring? The ring is brass stamped to look like 18K gold, worth pennies. Euro for Visitors reports the scam has been running continuously on Pont des Arts for over two decades. Ring-scammers work the same 100-meter stretch every single day, with multiple operators visible at peak tourist hours.
scams.avoidance: Say 'Non, merci' firmly and keep walking without slowing down. Never touch or accept the ring — the moment you hold it, you're 'obligated' in their script. Ignore anyone who bends down dramatically in front of you near tourist sites. If they follow you, walk toward a group of people, a police officer, or a nearby shop. Know that legitimate lost-and-found in France goes to the police commissariat, not random strangers. Keep hands in pockets or occupied with a phone/map so you can't receive the ring.
scams.location: Pont des Arts, along the Seine near the Louvre, Champ de Mars, Tuileries Gardens

scams.name: The Sacré-Cœur Friendship Bracelet Trap
scams.description: You're climbing the famous white steps toward Sacré-Cœur in Montmartre when a man suddenly grabs your wrist with a warm 'From where? America? Welcome, friend!' In about 20 seconds he has woven a colorful string bracelet around your fingers and tied it tight before you've said a word. The weaving goes fast — almost hypnotic — and then he's demanding €10, €20, sometimes €30, and his friends have quietly surrounded you. You can't take the bracelet off without cutting it, and they won't let you just walk away. Travel and Tour World (2024) reported this scam targeting the 10.5 million annual visitors to Sacré-Cœur. In 2014, Paris Police Commissioner Bernard Boucault was slapped by bracelet scammers when he tried to intervene — his chauffeur was punched and the head of public safety was kicked, demonstrating the organized violence behind the operation.
scams.avoidance: Keep your hands in your pockets or hold something (phone, bag strap) as you climb the Sacré-Cœur steps. Say a firm 'NON!' and pull your arm back the instant someone reaches for your wrist — do not let them make contact. Do not engage or make eye contact — looking away while walking is your best defense. If cornered, loudly say 'Appelez la police!' (Call the police) — they scatter instantly when attention is drawn. Visit Sacré-Cœur very early morning (before 8am) when the scammers haven't set up yet. Take the Montmartre funicular instead of the steps to avoid the gauntlet entirely. If a bracelet gets tied, refuse to pay and walk to the police officers stationed near Place du Tertre.
scams.location: Steps leading to Sacré-Cœur Basilica, Montmartre hilltop, Place du Tertre approaches

scams.name: The Deaf-Mute Petition Pickpocket
scams.description: You've just stepped off the RER at Champ de Mars and a young woman approaches holding a clipboard. She points to her ears and mouth — deaf-mute — and gestures for you to sign her petition for 'disabled children' or 'against drugs.' It seems harmless, even touching, so you sign. The moment the pen is back in her hand, she flips to a donation page showing previous 'donors' who gave €10, €20, €50 and points insistently. If you refuse, her accomplices have already lifted your phone from your back pocket while you were focused on the clipboard. At CDG airport, petition scammers attacked Aéroport de Paris workers who warned tourists about them. The operation runs on every major tourist corridor in Paris, with teams of 6-10 working in shifts.
scams.avoidance: Never sign anything from a stranger on the street in Paris — legitimate charities do not operate this way. Shake your head firmly, say 'Non,' and walk without breaking stride. If they block your path, step around them without engaging — say nothing. Be especially alert near the Eiffel Tower south entrance and Louvre courtyards. Keep your phone in a front zipped pocket, not a back pocket or loose bag. Travel with a companion and watch each other's bags when anyone approaches. Real French deaf organizations (like the Fédération Nationale des Sourds de France) do not solicit on the street.
scams.location: Eiffel Tower south entrance, Louvre pyramid courtyard, Champs-Élysées, Opéra Garnier steps, Notre-Dame area

scams.name: The Metro Door-Close Pickpocket Crush
scams.description: The doors of the Métro were about to close at Châtelet–Les Halles when three teenagers suddenly forced their way into an already-packed car, pressing everyone together. You felt the jostle but thought nothing of it — rush hour. Only at your stop did you reach for your phone and find your jacket pocket empty. The group had one person push you from the front while another lifted from behind. A 2016 investigation found a single gang was responsible for two-thirds of all metro thefts, employing approximately 100 young girls recruited from Eastern Europe with daily theft quotas of €300-€1,000. Paris generates more pickpocket-related travel reviews than any other city worldwide — 283 thefts per million tourists. The RER B from CDG airport is the single highest-risk corridor.
scams.avoidance: Keep valuables in a front zipped pocket, money belt, or inside jacket pocket — never outer or back pockets. Hold your bag in front of you on crowded trains, not slung to the side or back. If a group rushes the doors right at closing, let them pass and wait for the next train. Be extra vigilant at Châtelet, Gare du Nord, Opéra, and on RER B from CDG Airport. Consider a slim RFID-blocking wallet inside a shirt pocket for passport and cards. Keep one hand on your bag/pocket at all times in crowded cars. Board train cars near the driver's compartment where CCTV coverage is better.
scams.location: Metro Line 1 (Louvre, Champs-Élysées), Line 4 (Châtelet, Gare du Nord), RER B (CDG Airport to central Paris)

scams.name: The Fake Police Officer Wallet Check
scams.description: Two men in plain clothes flash what look like police badges near Pigalle and ask to see your passport — standard drug-check procedure, they say. Nervous about being stopped by French authorities, you hand it over. One 'officer' inspects your passport while the other asks to verify your wallet isn't carrying counterfeit bills. While you're focused on the document check, your wallet disappears or cash is palmed. Real Paris police in plain clothes rarely stop tourists for random passport checks without a uniformed officer present, and they will never ask to inspect your cash. The Bonjour Guide (2025) and multiple travel safety sites document this as an ongoing scam targeting tourists who don't know French police procedures.
scams.avoidance: Ask to be taken to the nearest commissariat (police station) — real officers will comply; scammers won't. Request a uniformed officer be present before showing any document. Keep your passport in your hotel safe and carry a photocopy plus your driver's license instead. Never open your wallet or show cash to anyone claiming to be police on the street. Call 17 (French emergency police line) immediately if you feel unsafe. Real French police carry a carte de police (police card) with photo, name, and badge number — ask to see it clearly. Walk toward a busy public area or shop if you feel threatened.
scams.location: Pigalle, near Moulin Rouge, backstreets near Opéra, Gare du Nord exits, tourist areas after dark

scams.name: The Tourist-Zone Restaurant Overcharge
scams.description: The menu outside the café near Notre-Dame showed a croque-monsieur for €8, and you sat down feeling pleased with the price. But the bill came to €34 — a €5 'couvert' (cover charge), the small bottled water you didn't order was €7, and the menu you'd seen was the 'lunch menu' that ended at noon. In July 2025, Le Parisien conducted a sting operation sending two journalists to the same Eiffel Tower-area restaurants — one dressed as a Parisian local, one as an American tourist in an Eiffel Tower t-shirt and baseball cap. The American was charged approximately 50% more across all restaurants tested. At one restaurant, the American received a larger Coke for €9.50 plus charged bottled water, while the 'local' got a small Coke for €6.50 and free tap water. At another, the waiter changed the American's tip from 10% to 15% and obscured the credit card machine screen. French law requires identical pricing regardless of language — charging tourists more is fraud.
scams.avoidance: Ask 'L'eau du robinet, s'il vous plaît' (tap water, please) immediately — it's free and legally required. Clarify 'C'est offert?' (Is this free?) when bread, olives, or nibbles are brought to the table. Check the full indoor menu and prices before sitting down. Walk 2-3 streets away from major monuments for better prices and authenticity. Check Google Maps reviews filtered by locals — 3.5 stars with 2000+ reviews often beats a polished tourist trap. Service charge (service compris) is legally included in all French restaurant prices — additional 'service charge' on the bill is fraudulent. Pay attention when entering your card PIN — some waiters try to change the tip amount.
scams.location: Restaurants within 500m of Eiffel Tower, Champs-Élysées side streets, Notre-Dame area, Montmartre Place du Tertre

scams.name: The Trocadéro Three-Card Monte
scams.description: A folding card table appeared near Trocadéro with a small crowd gathered around a fast-talking man shuffling three cups with a ball underneath. You watched someone in the crowd win €50 in seconds — easy money, right? You put down €20. The cup you tracked vanished and reappeared somewhere impossible. You lost. What you didn't realize: the 'winner' was a shill working with the dealer, the people cheering were accomplices, and the lookouts at the edge of the group would collapse the table and scatter if police appeared. In August 2025, a TikTok video of American tourist Nathalia Duques crying after losing 'so much money' to the Eiffel Tower three-card monte went viral with 11 million views. Commenters showed zero mercy: 'Imagine being scammed by 3 cups in 2025.' The game is mathematically impossible to win — the operator removes the ball during the shuffle using sleight of hand.
scams.avoidance: Never bet on street gambling — the game is mathematically and physically rigged; you cannot win. The 'winners' are part of the crew — their job is to make you think winning is possible. Walk past without stopping or watching — even spectating marks you as a potential target. If you've lost money, walk away immediately — trying to 'win it back' will only cost more. Report the location to police, but know that arrests are rare because operators move constantly. The sleight of hand is professional-grade — even knowing the trick, you cannot beat it.
scams.location: Trocadéro plaza, Pont d'Iéna (near Eiffel Tower), Champ de Mars riverbanks, Montmartre steps

scams.name: The CDG Airport Unlicensed Taxi Ambush
scams.description: You land at CDG exhausted from a transatlantic flight. In the arrivals hall, a well-dressed man approaches: 'Taxi? I take you to Paris, good price.' You agree to €70 — seems reasonable. But the 'taxi' is an unmarked car, there's no meter, and when you arrive at your hotel the driver demands €200, claiming traffic, tolls, and 'airport fees.' One traveler documented being charged €200 for a trip that should cost €56. Another was quoted €90 at CDG, then told it would be €120 upon arrival. At Gare du Nord, unlicensed operators quote €120+ for rides that official taxis do for €15-20. The official fixed rate from CDG is €56 to Right Bank, €65 to Left Bank — no exceptions, no 'extras.'
scams.avoidance: Only take taxis from the official queue outside baggage claim — look for the illuminated 'TAXI PARISIEN' roof sign. Know the official fixed rates: CDG to Right Bank €56, CDG to Left Bank €65, Orly to Paris €40-45. Use the G7 app or Uber/Bolt for pre-priced, tracked rides with driver ratings. If someone approaches inside the terminal, say 'Non merci' and walk to the official taxi stand. The RER B train from CDG to central Paris costs €11.80 and takes 35 minutes — the cheapest legitimate option. If a driver changes the price upon arrival, photograph their face and vehicle, refuse to pay the excess, and call 17. Official Paris taxis must run the meter for all rides except fixed airport routes.
scams.location: Charles de Gaulle Airport arrivals hall, Orly Airport exits, Gare du Nord Eurostar exit

scams.name: The Gare du Nord Station Gauntlet
scams.description: You step off the Eurostar into Gare du Nord, Europe's busiest station, and immediately you're approached: someone offers to help with tickets, another wants to take your photo, a third bumps into you while pointing at a map. Gare du Nord is the most-reported theft location in Paris. One scam involves men with fake ID badges offering to help you buy metro tickets with their bank card, then demanding you pay €20+ in cash for a €2.15 ticket. Another uses the 'photo' request to position you in a dark corner while accomplices separate you from your luggage. The station's chaotic confluence of Eurostar, Thalys, RER, metro, and bus connections creates perfect cover for organized pickpocket teams.
scams.avoidance: Buy tickets from official machines (they have English option) or the SNCF/RATP counter — never from helpful strangers. Keep rolling luggage handle in hand and bag straps across body at all times. Walk with purpose directly to the metro/RER entrance or taxi queue — don't stop in the main hall. If someone approaches, say 'Non merci' and keep walking without engaging. Unofficial taxis congregate outside Eurostar exits — walk past them to the official taxi rank. Know your connection before arriving — check the RATP app for metro directions. The station has police presence, but pickpockets are skilled at avoiding detection.

scams.name: The Phone Snatch at Metro Doors
scams.description: You're standing near the metro doors scrolling through Google Maps when the departure chime sounds. In the split second before the doors close, a hand reaches in, snatches your phone, and the thief is on the platform as the train pulls away. By the time you process what happened, you're halfway to the next station. This is the most common phone theft method in Paris — perfectly timed to the door-closing sequence so victims have no chance to react or pursue. In 2025, a new variant emerged targeting tourists who wear phones on long lanyards around their neck, with thieves cutting the cord in crowded cars. Phone theft in the Métro is now the number one petty crime in Paris.
scams.avoidance: Never use your phone near metro doors — step away from the door area when checking maps or messages. Keep your phone in a zipped front pocket, not in hand or dangling from a lanyard, especially when standing. If you must check your phone, turn your back to a wall or pole so no one can approach from behind. Be extra vigilant when the door-closing chime sounds — this is prime snatch time. Enable Find My iPhone/Google Find My Device and remote wipe before your trip. Consider a reinforced phone case with wrist loop (not neck lanyard) for secure grip. Sit rather than stand when possible, keeping the phone on your lap or in a closed bag.
scams.location: All Paris metro lines, especially at Châtelet, République, Gare de Lyon, and tourist-heavy stations

scams.name: The ATM Distraction & Skim
scams.description: You're withdrawing cash from an ATM near the Champs-Élysées when someone taps your shoulder: 'Excuse me, you dropped this €20.' You turn, and in that moment your card is swapped for a similar one, or your PIN is observed by an accomplice, or skimming hardware records your card details. Some Paris ATMs, particularly private (non-bank) machines near tourist sites, have been found with skimming devices attached. A March 2025 DailyMail report found one in ten tourists to France (212,000 people over five years) admitted to being scammed, with ATM fraud a significant contributor.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours — these are monitored and maintained. Cover the keypad completely with your other hand when entering your PIN. Before inserting your card, wiggle the card slot and keypad — skimmers are often loosely attached. Ignore anyone who approaches you mid-transaction — complete or cancel immediately. Use contactless payment wherever possible to reduce ATM usage. Enable transaction alerts on your banking app for immediate fraud detection. Avoid private/independent ATMs in tourist areas — stick to major French banks (BNP Paribas, Crédit Agricole, Société Générale).
scams.location: Standalone ATMs in tourist areas, non-bank ATMs near attractions, machines in dimly lit locations

scams.name: The Rose Seller Restaurant Shakedown
scams.description: You're enjoying a romantic dinner at an outdoor terrace when someone approaches with a basket of roses. 'For your beautiful lady?' He places a rose in her hand or on the table before you can respond. Now he demands €10, €15, even €20 for a single flower that cost him centimes. If you refuse, he becomes loud and aggressive, creating a scene that embarrasses you in front of your date and the surrounding diners. Some victims report rose sellers returning repeatedly throughout the meal, despite initial refusals. The sellers know tourists will often pay just to end the confrontation.
scams.avoidance: Say 'Non merci' firmly before the rose is placed down — don't let them put it on the table. Do not touch the rose — once you've touched it, they'll claim you've 'accepted' it. If a rose is placed down unwanted, leave it on the table and continue ignoring the seller. Request restaurant staff intervene if the seller becomes aggressive. Indoor seating eliminates the issue entirely — sellers don't enter restaurants. A firm, repeated 'Non' without further engagement usually ends the interaction.
scams.location: Outdoor restaurant terraces in Le Marais, Latin Quarter, Montmartre, along the Seine

scams.name: The Fake Airbnb Phantom Listing
scams.description: You found the perfect Paris apartment — 2 bedrooms near the Marais for €100/night, beautiful photos, great reviews. The 'host' contacted you outside Airbnb, offering a 15% discount for direct bank transfer. You paid €700 for a week. When you arrived, the address didn't exist, the host's phone was disconnected, and Airbnb's support couldn't help because the transaction happened off-platform. During the 2024 Olympics, multiple tourists arrived in Paris to find their 'confirmed' rentals were fake listings, leaving them homeless during the world's biggest sporting event. Airbnb removed 59,000 fake listings in response to the epidemic.
scams.avoidance: NEVER pay outside of Airbnb's platform — the only protection is their payment system. Verify the exact address exists using Google Street View before booking. Read reviews carefully — look for specific details about the apartment, not generic praise. Reverse image search listing photos to check if they appear elsewhere. Book with Superhosts who have long track records and many detailed reviews. If a deal seems too good to be true for central Paris, it is. Report suspicious listings to Airbnb immediately.
scams.location: Online (Airbnb lookalike sites, Facebook Marketplace, WhatsApp contacts), with fake addresses across Paris

scams.name: The 'Clumsy Jogger' Bump-and-Lift
scams.description: You're walking through the Tuileries when a jogger collides with you from behind — apologizing profusely, checking if you're okay, brushing off your jacket. By the time they've jogged away, your phone is gone from your pocket. The 'clumsy jogger' is a classic distraction technique: the physical contact masks the lift, and the apology buys time for an accomplice or for the jogger themselves to create distance. Variations include someone dropping items at your feet, 'accidentally' spilling coffee on you, or asking you to help with a heavy map while their partner works your pockets.
scams.avoidance: If bumped, immediately check your pockets and bag while keeping eyes on the person. Don't let strangers touch your clothing to 'clean' spills — step back and handle it yourself. Keep valuables in zipped front pockets, not back pockets or open bags. Travel with a companion who can watch your belongings during any distraction. Be especially alert in parks and gardens where 'joggers' have plausible cover. If something feels wrong, loudly say 'Non!' and create distance.
scams.location: Jardin des Tuileries, Luxembourg Gardens, Seine riverbanks, jogging paths near tourist areas
sources: City Paris 'Street Scams in Paris 2025': documents the clumsy jogger/bump technique

scams.name: Restaurant Racketeering & Minimum Spend
scams.description: St-Tropez restaurants have developed sophisticated systems to extract maximum spending from tourists. Restaurants compile secret databases tracking how much each diner spends and tips. If you don't spend or tip enough, you'll be blacklisted and refused a table on your next visit. Some establishments demand €5,000 minimum spending or €1,500 per head just to secure a reservation. Despite service charges already being included, staff aggressively pressure tourists for additional 'American-style' tips. In one notorious incident, a waiter chased an Italian customer into the parking lot demanding he return inside to add another €500 to his already €500 tip. The mayor of Saint-Tropez has publicly condemned these practices as 'racketeering.'
scams.avoidance: Research restaurant policies and reviews before booking. Ask explicitly about minimum spending requirements upfront. Remember that service charge is already included in France. Choose smaller local establishments over famous beach clubs.
scams.location: Beach clubs, High-end restaurants, Port area restaurants

scams.name: Luxury Watch Theft
scams.description: Organized criminal groups systematically target tourists wearing expensive watches worth €100,000+. The operation is sophisticated: spotters identify valuable timepieces, then communicate with thieves who steal the watch—subtly or violently—before escaping on mopeds with tampered plates. Three separate incidents in St-Tropez resulted in €400,000 worth of stolen watches in a single weekend. These thefts are becoming increasingly brazen and sometimes violent.
scams.avoidance: Leave valuable watches worth over €5,000 at home. If wearing expensive watches, keep them covered. Stay aware of your surroundings, especially near beach areas. Report suspicious behavior to police immediately.
scams.location: Pampelonne Beach, Beach restaurants, Port area, Yacht clubs, Town center

scams.name: Villa Rental Fraud
scams.description: Scammers create attractive listings for luxury villas that either don't exist or aren't theirs to rent. They use professional photos stolen from legitimate listings and below-market prices to lure victims. Travelers book and pay via wire transfer, only to arrive and discover the property doesn't exist or someone else has already rented it. Fake booking forms designed to look like Airbnb confirmations direct money to fraudulent accounts.
scams.avoidance: Use only established concierge services and rental agencies. Perform reverse image searches on property photos. Never pay via wire transfer—use credit card for protection. Be suspicious of deals that seem too good to be true.
scams.location: Online booking platforms

scams.name: Hotel Room Burglary
scams.description: Professional burglars target luxury hotel rooms, particularly those with terrace access. In one case, two British women lost nearly €1 million in valuables—including 11 Hermès Birkin bags, Patek Philippe watches, and Cartier jewelry—after their five-star hotel room was ransacked within hours of check-in. The thieves broke through the private terrace door and tore the safe from the wall. A hotel employee was questioned, suggesting possible inside involvement.
scams.avoidance: Don't bring valuables worth more than €5,000. Request upper floor rooms without easy exterior access. Keep valuable items with you when possible. Consider travel insurance that covers theft.
scams.location: Luxury hotels, Villas with private terraces

scams.name: Gas Burglary (Villa Gassing)
scams.description: Criminals allegedly pump anesthetic gas through air conditioning vents or windows to sedate sleeping occupants before robbing them. Notable victims include F1 driver Jenson Button and TV presenter Richard Hammond. Police estimate 90% of villa raids go unreported. However, medical experts dispute whether such 'knock-out gas' actually exists as described.
scams.avoidance: Choose upper floor accommodations. Lock all windows and terrace doors. Don't sleep with windows open. Consider portable door alarms.
scams.location: Rental villas, Hotel rooms with external ventilation access

scams.name: Beach Club Overcharging
scams.description: Beach clubs employ questionable practices. Sun loungers cost €35-50 each, and famous clubs like Nikki Beach require €1,500 minimum spend on weekends during high season. Despite websites stating prices include service charges, staff express dissatisfaction with tip amounts. To get weekend reservations at exclusive clubs like Club 55, guests may need to 'tip' waiters in advance.
scams.avoidance: Research prices and minimum spend requirements before visiting. Ask for prices upfront before ordering. Remember service charge is already included. Consider less famous beach clubs.
scams.location: Pampelonne Beach, Club 55, Nikki Beach

scams.name: Boat/Yacht Rental Hidden Fees
scams.description: Boat rental companies advertise attractive daily rates but add substantial hidden costs: fuel (St-Tropez has notably higher diesel prices), delivery/redelivery fees, mooring fees, and water sports equipment charges. Captain fees vary widely—standard rate is €350, but some quote €500+ without justification. Additional unexpected charges may appear for 'gourmet lunch' or mandatory insurance add-ons.
scams.avoidance: Get complete all-inclusive pricing in writing before booking. Compare total costs including fuel across companies. Ask specifically about all potential additional charges.
scams.location: Port of St-Tropez, Marina, Online booking platforms

scams.name: Pickpocketing & Distraction Theft
scams.description: Professional pickpockets operate in crowded tourist areas during summer. Organized gangs use distraction techniques—one member causes a commotion while others target your valuables. Some teams use the 'petition/clipboard approach.' Scooter thieves may grab bags or phones from pedestrians. The Tuesday and Saturday markets at Place des Lices are particularly high-risk.
scams.avoidance: Keep bags zipped and in front of you. Don't carry bags on your street-side shoulder. Use money belts or hidden pouches. Be extra vigilant in crowded market areas.
scams.location: Place des Lices Market, Port area, Crowded restaurants, Beach areas

scams.name: Taxi Overcharging
scams.description: Unlicensed and some licensed taxi drivers target tourists with inflated fares. Common tactics include claiming the meter is broken, taking long routes, or forcing cash payment. Airport transfers from Nice to St-Tropez legitimately cost €240-275 (day) or €265-285 (night), but scammers may quote much higher.
scams.avoidance: Use only official taxis from designated stands. Research standard fares before arrival. Use ride-sharing apps like Uber for tracked journeys. Pre-book airport transfers through hotels.
scams.location: Nice Airport transfers, Town center, Beach areas

scams.name: Jet Ski Rental Damage Scam
scams.description: Some jet ski rental operators make false damage claims after rental. After you return the jet ski, they claim you damaged it and demand large sums for repairs—often under threats and coercion. If you refuse to pay, you may be threatened with police, where 'administrative charges' inflate the demanded amount further.
scams.avoidance: Photograph/video the jet ski from all angles before rental. Ensure date/time stamps are visible in documentation. Never surrender your passport as collateral. Research operators thoroughly—check online reviews.
scams.location: Beaches, Water sports rental areas, Port Grimaud

scams.name: Contactless Card Skimming
scams.description: Thieves use digital skimming devices to steal money from contactless-enabled cards without physical contact. They carry concealed readers that capture card information when held close to your wallet or purse in crowded areas, allowing fraudulent purchases or card cloning.
scams.avoidance: Use RFID-blocking wallets or card sleeves. Keep cards in front pockets or secure inner pockets. Regularly monitor card statements for unauthorized charges. Set up transaction alerts on your banking app.
scams.location: Crowded areas, Markets, Public transport

scams.name: Fake Charity Petitions
scams.description: Scammers approach tourists with clipboards asking them to sign petitions for fake charities. While you're distracted reading and signing, an accomplice targets your bag or pockets. Even if no theft occurs, you may be pressured to donate money to a non-existent cause.
scams.avoidance: Politely refuse and keep walking. Never stop to engage with clipboard wielders. Keep your belongings secure if you do stop.
scams.location: Place des Lices, Port area, Tourist walkways

scams.name: Petition/Deaf Charity Clipboard Scam
scams.description: Teams of scammers approach tourists with clipboards asking if they speak English, then request signatures for a fake 'deaf charity' petition. While you're distracted reading or signing, accomplices pickpocket your bags or pockets. After signing, they demand a donation, pointing to text claiming you agreed to donate. The petition is always in English (a red flag in France) and they use exaggerated sign language to appear hearing-impaired.
scams.avoidance: Never stop for clipboard petitioners. Say 'Non' firmly and keep walking. Never sign anything on the street. Keep hands on your belongings when approached.
scams.location: Strasbourg Cathedral, Cathedral Square, Place Kléber, Petite France, Train Station

scams.name: Friendship Bracelet/String Scam
scams.description: A vendor grabs your hand and begins wrapping colorful string around your wrist before you can refuse. Within seconds, they've tied a difficult-to-remove bracelet and demand €10-20 for the 'gift.' They become aggressive if you refuse to pay, and may follow you while creating a scene. Sometimes an accomplice uses the distraction to pickpocket you.
scams.avoidance: Keep hands in pockets when walking through tourist areas. Say 'Non' firmly and keep walking. Pull your hand away immediately if they try to grab it. Carry small scissors to cut yourself free if necessary.
scams.location: Cathedral steps, Petite France, Tourist walkways, Christmas markets

scams.name: Gold Ring Scam
scams.description: A stranger bends down near you and 'finds' a gold ring, then asks if you dropped it. When you say no, they examine it and claim it's marked '18K gold' and must be valuable. They offer to sell it for a fraction of its 'worth' or ask for a finder's fee. The ring is worthless brass. While engaging you, an accomplice may be pickpocketing you.
scams.avoidance: Simply say 'non' and walk away. Don't engage in conversation. Be aware of accomplices nearby. Keep hands on belongings.
scams.location: Near bridges, Pedestrian areas, Tourist walkways, Pont du Corbeau

scams.name: Tram/Public Transport Pickpocketing
scams.description: Pickpockets work the crowded Strasbourg trams, especially Lines B and C that serve tourist areas. They operate during rush hours and at boarding/exiting when movement is chaotic. Teams use distraction techniques—one person blocks your path or bumps into you while an accomplice steals from your bag or pocket. They often exit quickly just as doors close.
scams.avoidance: Keep bags in front with hands on them. Don't keep valuables in back pockets. Be extra vigilant when boarding and exiting. If bumped, immediately check belongings.
scams.location: Tram Lines B and C, Gare Centrale, Crowded tram stops, Cathedral area tram stops

scams.name: Counterfeit Attraction Tickets
scams.description: Unlicensed sellers approach tourists outside popular attractions offering 'discounted' tickets for boat tours, cathedral tower climbs, or other experiences. The tickets are fake, already used, or for non-existent tours. The seller disappears before you discover the scam. Some pose as official guides offering 'special access.'
scams.avoidance: Buy tickets only from official ticket offices. Book tours through established companies. Be suspicious of 'special deals' from strangers. Research official prices beforehand.
scams.location: Near Strasbourg Cathedral, Boat tour departure points, Outside tourist attractions

scams.name: Christmas Market Pickpocketing
scams.description: Strasbourg's famous Christmas markets attract over 2 million visitors annually, creating ideal conditions for pickpockets. The dense crowds, distracting lights, and hands occupied with food and drinks make tourists easy targets. Professional teams work the markets, using distraction techniques or simply taking advantage of the chaos. Valuable items disappear from bags, pockets, and even hands.
scams.avoidance: Wear cross-body bags in front. Keep zippers secured and hands on bags. Leave valuables at hotel. Be extra vigilant in crowded market lanes. Visit during less crowded morning hours.
scams.location: Christkindelsmärik (main market), Place Broglie, Place Kléber, All Christmas market locations

scams.name: Taxi Meter Manipulation
scams.description: Some taxi drivers target tourists unfamiliar with local fares. They may claim the meter is broken and quote inflated prices, take unnecessarily long routes, or select the higher night/weekend tariff during regular hours. From the airport to city center, legitimate fare is approximately €40-50 during the day.
scams.avoidance: Insist on using the meter. Know the approximate fare in advance. Use GPS to follow the route. Consider using Uber or official taxi apps. Get receipt for any disputes.
scams.location: Strasbourg Airport, Gare Centrale, Hotel pickups at night

scams.name: Fake Police/Document Check Scam
scams.description: Criminals pose as plainclothes police, quickly flashing fake badges. They claim they need to check your wallet for counterfeit currency or verify your identity due to 'border security.' While examining your wallet or documents, they steal cash. Being near the German border, they may claim special authority for 'cross-border checks.' Real French police don't randomly check tourists' wallets on the street.
scams.avoidance: Ask to see official ID clearly and note badge number. Insist on going to nearest police station before showing documents. Never hand over your wallet to anyone on the street. Call 17 (police) if suspicious.
scams.location: Tourist areas, Near borders, Tram stops, Quiet streets at night

scams.name: Restaurant Menu Overcharging
scams.description: Tourist restaurants near major attractions use tactics to overcharge visitors. Different menus in different languages show different prices. Waiters bring expensive bottled water without asking, add items not ordered, or charge premium prices for Alsatian specialties. Some insist on automatic gratuity despite service being included in French prices.
scams.avoidance: Ask for the French menu and compare prices. Request 'une carafe d'eau' (tap water) - it's free. Check bill carefully against what you ordered. Know that service is included in French prices. Walk a few streets from major monuments for better value.
scams.location: Cathedral Square restaurants, Petite France terraces, Tourist-heavy areas

scams.name: ATM Skimming
scams.description: Criminals attach skimming devices to ATMs that capture card data and PINs. Private ATMs like Euronet charge excessive fees and poor exchange rates. Some offer Dynamic Currency Conversion at terrible rates while making it seem like a benefit. Card trap devices may also be used - your card gets stuck and a 'helpful' stranger watches you enter your PIN.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside bank branches only. Cover keypad when entering PIN. Wiggle card slot before inserting. Decline dynamic currency conversion. If card gets stuck, don't leave - call bank immediately.
scams.location: Standalone ATMs, ATMs in tourist areas, Private ATMs (Euronet, Travelex)

scams.name: Bump and Grab/Distraction Theft
scams.description: A well-dressed person 'accidentally' bumps into you, spills something on you, or drops items near your feet. While apologizing profusely and helping clean you up or as you helpfully bend down to assist, an accomplice steals from your bag or pockets. Another variation: someone points out a 'stain' on your back to distract you.
scams.avoidance: If spilled on, immediately check belongings and move away. Don't let strangers touch your clothing. Be suspicious of any unusual contact. Keep bags secured in front of you.
scams.location: Crowded tourist areas, Cathedral entrances, Tram stops, Markets

scams.name: Street Vendor Overcharging
scams.description: Unlicensed vendors sell cheap souvenirs, 'artwork,' or photos at massively inflated prices. They target tourists at photo spots, offering to take pictures then demanding payment for the 'service.' Some sell 'authentic Alsatian' items that are actually mass-produced imports. They become aggressive when you refuse to buy or try to negotiate.
scams.avoidance: Buy souvenirs from established shops. Decline offers from street vendors. Never hand your camera/phone to unsolicited helpers. Know that most legitimate vendors have fixed prices displayed.
scams.location: Near Cathedral, Tourist photo spots, Petite France bridges

scams.name: String/Bracelet Friendship Scam
scams.description: Near Basilique Saint-Sernin, a vendor approaches tourists and ties a string or friendship bracelet around your wrist, claiming it is a 'cadeau' (gift). Once attached, they aggressively demand payment, often blocking your path until you pay. The bracelet is nearly impossible to remove quickly.
scams.avoidance: Keep hands in pockets when approached. Say 'Non merci' firmly and keep walking without stopping. Never let anyone tie anything on your wrist.
scams.location: Basilique Saint-Sernin, Place du Capitole

scams.name: Gold Ring Scam
scams.description: By the Canal du Midi or in tourist areas, a passer-by 'finds' a ring on the ground near you and claims it is 18-karat gold. They offer to sell it for 'gas money.' While you are distracted, an accomplice rifles through your bags or pockets. The ring is worthless brass.
scams.avoidance: Ignore any found jewelry and walk away immediately. Head toward the nearest busy cafe or shop if someone persists. Never engage in conversation about found items.
scams.location: Canal du Midi, tourist pedestrian areas, river quays

scams.name: Fake Petition/Deaf-Mute Charity Scam
scams.description: Young people, often pretending to be deaf-mute, approach tourists with clipboards asking for signatures on petitions for fake charities. After signing, they reveal a mandatory donation of 10-20 euros. Meanwhile, accomplices may pickpocket distracted victims.
scams.avoidance: Firmly say 'No' and walk away without stopping. Never sign anything on the street. These are organized groups and the money never goes to charity.
scams.location: Place du Capitole, Basilique Saint-Sernin, tourist attractions

scams.name: Metro and Public Transport Pickpocketing
scams.description: Pickpockets operate throughout Toulouse's metro system and buses, particularly during crowded rush hours. They work in groups where one person creates a distraction or crowding while accomplices steal wallets, phones, and valuables.
scams.avoidance: Keep valuables in front pockets or secure cross-body bags. Be especially vigilant during boarding and exiting when crowds press together. Use money belts for large amounts of cash.
scams.location: Metro lines throughout city, bus stops, metro stations

scams.name: Gare Matabiau Train Station Theft
scams.description: Thefts and muggings are more common around Toulouse's central train station, Gare Matabiau, than in other parts of the city. The area between Rue Bayard and Allees Jean Jaures is particularly risky. Luggage theft and distraction pickpocketing are primary concerns.
scams.avoidance: Stay alert at the station and surrounding streets. Keep luggage close and use locks on bags. Avoid walking alone late at night. Use official taxi stands or pre-booked transport.
scams.location: Gare Matabiau, Rue Bayard, Allees Jean Jaures

scams.name: Fake Police ID Scam
scams.description: A stranger approaches asking you to break a large bill. Soon after, a 'police officer' appears with a story about illegal money exchange and asks to see your wallet for 'inspection.' They return it with half your cash missing. Scammers may wear armbands and carry fake badges.
scams.avoidance: Real French police never ask to see your wallet - only your ID removed from the wallet. Never hand over your wallet or phone. Ask to see police credentials and offer to walk to the nearest police station. If suspicious, dial 17.
scams.location: Metro stations, tourist areas, near ATMs

scams.name: Taxi Overcharging and Scams
scams.description: Some taxi drivers attempt to overcharge tourists by using nighttime tariffs during the day, taking unnecessarily long routes, or claiming the meter is broken. Unofficial taxis without proper markings may charge exorbitant rates.
scams.avoidance: Use only official taxis with clearly marked 'TAXI' signs, visible taximeters, and displayed driver details. Ask for an estimate before starting and confirm the route. Note driver numbers if overcharged.
scams.location: Toulouse-Blagnac Airport, Gare Matabiau, city center

scams.name: Restaurant Tourist Trap Menu Scam
scams.description: Some restaurants offer cheap set menus displayed outside but present different, more expensive menus once seated. Other tactics include menus without prices, pushing medium or large portions only, and serving bottled water without asking. Some bars present inflated bills and use intimidation.
scams.avoidance: Check prices before ordering and confirm them verbally. Avoid restaurants with menus in many languages. Request the same menu shown outside. Always ask for 'une carafe d'eau' (tap water) which is free. Review your bill carefully.
scams.location: Place du Capitole, tourist-heavy streets, near major attractions

scams.name: ATM Skimming and Card Fraud
scams.description: Criminals install skimming devices on ATMs that capture card data and PINs. Automated service stations and ATMs in tourist areas are frequently targeted. Some scammers approach ATM users offering to 'help' while watching PIN entry or claiming the machine is broken to steal inserted cards.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours. Cover the keypad completely when entering your PIN. Check for loose or unusual attachments on card slots. Never accept help from strangers at ATMs.
scams.location: Standalone ATMs, tourist areas, automated service stations

scams.name: Rose Seller Distraction Theft
scams.description: A scammer approaches with roses, offering one as a 'free gift.' Once you accept or touch it, they refuse to take it back and aggressively demand payment. While distracted by the confrontation, an accomplice quietly pickpockets your wallet, phone, or bag.
scams.avoidance: Never accept items from street vendors. Keep hands in pockets and say 'Non merci' firmly without breaking stride. Be aware of anyone positioning behind you during such encounters.
scams.location: Restaurant terraces, Place du Capitole, tourist areas

scams.name: Canal-Side Bicycle Grab Theft
scams.description: Thieves on bicycles target outdoor diners along the Canal du Midi and river quays. They rapidly grab phones, cameras, and bags from tables as they cycle past, making pursuit nearly impossible. The theft happens in seconds, often before victims can react.
scams.avoidance: Sit with your back against walls, facing outward. Never leave phones on tablecloths or table edges. Use wrist straps when filming or photographing. Keep bags on your lap or looped around chair legs.
scams.location: Canal du Midi, river quays, outdoor restaurant terraces

scams.name: Shell Game / Three-Card Monte
scams.description: A street operator sets up a game with three cups and a ball, shuffling quickly and inviting passersby to bet on finding the ball. The entire crowd including 'winners' are planted accomplices. The game uses sleight of hand making it impossible to win. While attention is focused on the game, accomplices pickpocket the crowd.
scams.avoidance: Never stop for street gambling games - they are illegal and always rigged. Walk away immediately if you see a crowd gathered around such games. Keep valuables secured.
scams.location: Busy pedestrian areas, tourist zones
